rubric.task_read: A long-horizon software port: reimplement a large Java network-visualization tool (BioFabric) plus its alignment plugin as a Rust library + CLI, achieving byte-level parity with the Java reference across visible AND held-out test suites. Difficulty comes from reverse-engineering exact Java algorithms (node/edge ordering, layout, output formatting) where any subtle tie-break or byte differs, and from a fixed public API skeleton with many todo!() stubs. This warrants heavy, sustained meta-work: deep source-tracing of the reference, careful sequencing of dependent components, verification that localizes byte discrepancies, and disciplined correction rather than guess-and-check against goldens.

dimensions.name: Reference-source reverse engineering
dimensions.description: Reading and tracing the Java BioFabric/AlignmentPlugin source to understand the exact algorithms and output formats before/while implementing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Byte-level parity is impossible to hit by guessing from signatures and test names; the only ground truth for ordering, tie-breaks, and formatting lives in the Java source, so accurate understanding of it gates every deliverable.

anchors.0: Implements against skeleton signatures / test names / golden fragments without opening the Java reference at all.
anchors.3: Skims a Java file once for the feature being coded; relies mostly on guessing output shape from goldens.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Java classes for each feature before implementing it, extracting the core algorithm correctly for the common case.
anchors.8: Systematically maps Java classes to Rust modules, traces the exact code paths that emit output, and identifies ordering/tie-break/formatting rules (not just the happy path) directly from source.
anchors.10: Sustained, precise source archaeology: pins down subtle determinants of byte output (iteration order, sort stability, numeric/string formatting, edge cases in the alignment plugin), cross-references call sites, and re-consults the source as new discrepancies reveal gaps in understanding.

dimensions.name: Component sequencing & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered sub-goals (parsing, core model, layout, ordering, CLI, alignment) with explicit done-checks, respecting dependencies.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Many interdependent components feed the same outputs; building layout before a correct model, or CLI before core, wastes effort and produces cascading parity failures, so ordered milestones with clear completion signals sustain progress.

anchors.0: Attacks stubs in arbitrary order with no visible plan; jumps between unrelated components.
anchors.3: Loosely goes test-by-test with no dependency reasoning; foundations and dependents interleaved haphazardly.
anchors.5: Groups work sensibly (e.g., parsing/model first, then layout, then CLI) and finishes coherent chunks before moving on.
anchors.8: Explicit ordered milestones tied to concrete done-checks (specific test groups green), sequenced so each unblocks the next and shared primitives are built once.
anchors.10: Clear dependency-aware milestone hierarchy that anticipates which components share output-formatting logic, sequences the hardest parity-critical pieces early, and adjusts the milestone map as the true structure of the Java code emerges.

dimensions.name: Parity verification & discrepancy localization
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing how to confirm byte-level correctness — diffing against goldens/Java, localizing where output first diverges — beyond just running the given tests.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A held-out suite means passing visible goldens is necessary but insufficient; the agent needs verification that isolates the exact source of a byte mismatch and confirms the true algorithm, not just green visible tests.

anchors.0: Assumes code is correct; rarely runs the suite; no diffing when output mismatches.
anchors.3: Runs provided tests and eyeballs pass/fail, but on a mismatch retries blindly without pinpointing where bytes diverge.
anchors.5: Runs the relevant test groups iteratively and inspects diff output to find the first mismatching region before fixing.
anchors.8: Byte-level diffing to localize discrepancies precisely, and cross-checks behavior against the Java reference (or its expected output) rather than only the golden, to validate the underlying rule.
anchors.10: Builds/uses a repeatable comparison harness (e.g., generating novel inputs and comparing Rust vs Java behavior) to guard against held-out failures, systematically verifying edge cases and formatting invariants the visible goldens don't cover.

dimensions.name: Test-landscape progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of which test groups pass/remain across the whole suite and detecting stuck/circular debugging.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With many tests and a stubborn class of byte-parity bugs, losing track of done-vs-remaining or looping on one failing case wastes the horizon and risks regressions in already-passing areas.

anchors.0: No sense of overall status; unaware how many tests pass or what's left.
anchors.3: Occasional full runs but no running model of remaining work; surprised by regressions.
anchors.5: Periodically runs the workspace suite and keeps a rough, mostly-accurate tally of passing vs failing groups.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate done/remaining picture across parity/analysis/CLI suites, watches for regressions in passing areas, and recognizes when a single bug is consuming disproportionate cycles.
anchors.10: Continuously calibrated progress model across the horizon; explicitly detects thrashing/circular fixes on a stubborn parity bug and steps back to re-diagnose rather than re-attempting variations.

dimensions.name: Model-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising the mental model / approach when a parity result contradicts an assumed Java behavior, rather than tweaking blindly toward the golden.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Parity failures usually mean the agent's model of the Java algorithm is wrong; the productive response is to return to the source and correct the model, not to patch outputs until a specific golden matches (which fails held-out cases).

anchors.0: Repeats the same failing approach or hardcodes toward the golden regardless of why it diverged.
anchors.3: Makes surface tweaks in response to failures without questioning whether the underlying algorithm model is wrong.
anchors.5: When a fix doesn't work, forms a new hypothesis and tests it, occasionally revisiting the source.
anchors.8: Treats a persistent mismatch as evidence the model is wrong, returns to the Java source to correct it, and updates related code consistently.
anchors.10: Recognizes when a whole component's approach is mis-derived (e.g., wrong layout/ordering algorithm) and restructures decisively, abandoning guess-and-check loops in favor of source-grounded correction that also fixes latent held-out cases.

dimensions.name: Faithful implementation vs golden overfitting
dimensions.description: Strategically choosing to implement the true algorithm (so held-out networks pass) rather than special-casing or hardcoding to satisfy visible goldens.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly warns of a held-out suite and demands a faithful rewrite; an agent that optimizes only for visible goldens will silently fail hidden cases, so the meta-decision to generalize is itself a distinct quality signal.

anchors.0: Hardcodes outputs or pattern-matches on known test inputs to force visible goldens green.
anchors.3: Frequently special-cases to pass a specific golden without deriving the general rule.
anchors.5: Generally implements real logic, with occasional shortcuts that would not generalize.
anchors.8: Consistently implements the general algorithm from the source, explicitly avoiding golden-specific shortcuts, aware that held-out inputs must also pass.
anchors.10: Treats the visible goldens as samples of a general contract, deliberately validating that the implementation is input-agnostic and stress-testing generality, so held-out networks are covered by construction.
